Urban Heat Vulnerability Index · Poland

Where heat meets the people least able to withstand it

A 1 km index across all of Poland, combining five summers of Landsat surface temperature with census age structure, tree cover, sealed ground and surface water. It ranks 302 cities — and the biggest are not the worst.

Grid NSP2021, 1 km, 315,857 cells Heat Landsat 8/9 L2 ST, summers 2021–2025 Land cover Copernicus HRL + BDOT10k By Anastasiia Morozova Built 28 July 2026

The national picture

Vulnerability is concentrated, not diffuse. Cities burn red against a cooler countryside, and the mountains in the south — the Tatras and Sudetes — are the coolest inhabited land in Poland. Colour is the national quintile of the index, so a red cell is in the worst fifth of all inhabited cells.

What drives each city

The index is the mean of three equally weighted parts. Segments are drawn to scale and labelled directly, so the mix is readable without relying on colour alone.

Exposure — summer surface heat Sensitivity — children and over-65s Cooling deficit — missing trees, water, permeable ground

Exposure separates the cities; sensitivity barely does

Sensitivity sits above 0.9 in almost every large city — dense urban cells all reach the top of the national density distribution, so the term stops discriminating between them. The ranking is therefore driven mostly by exposure and cooling deficit.

The same index, city by city

Each tile is roughly 25–35 km across at 1 km resolution, on the national colour scale. Bydgoszcz and Poznań are almost solidly in the top quintile; Kraków and Gdynia break up into cooler river, park and coastal cells.

Big cities are not the worst

Ranked against all 302 Polish cities, the voivodeship capitals scatter from 5th to 168th. The ten worst cities in the country are mostly mid-sized towns in Wielkopolska and Lower Silesia — sealed, low-canopy and demographically old — that a study of major cities alone would never surface.

Where the capitals land:

Method and limits

  • Index. Mean of exposure, sensitivity and cooling deficit, each scaled 0–1 against the 2nd–98th percentile of all inhabited Polish cells. Densities are log-transformed first — population density is log-normal, and scaling it linearly pushes half of all cells below 0.1.
  • It is relative, not absolute. A value of 0.9 means "worse than almost everywhere else in Poland", not a probability of harm. Cities cannot all be low; the scale is defined by the cells in it.
  • Land-surface temperature is not air temperature. Landsat measures what the ground radiates at roughly 10am. It locates hot urban surfaces, not what a thermometer reads at head height.
  • Sensitivity saturates. Roughly a quarter of cells in the largest cities sit at the ceiling of the density scale, so the index does not distinguish degrees of density among them.
  • Age suppression. GUS withholds age counts in sparsely populated cells; those stay null rather than zero. Cells with complete age data still hold 98% of the population.
  • One coverage gap, partly interpolated. A 25–30 km north–south stripe around Kalisz, Konin and Turek carries no surface temperature in any Landsat scene — 0 of 12 tested, including cloud-free acquisitions on both orbital paths across all five summers. The hole is fixed in geography rather than time, so it is a systematic retrieval failure in the product, not weather, and more scenes cannot close it. cells were filled by inverse-distance interpolation from valid neighbours within 20 km, which is defensible only because the area is flat, agricultural and homogeneous. Filled cells carry lst_interpolated = 1 and every figure here is reproducible with them excluded. A further 815 cells were refused because their neighbours disagreed by more than 3 °C — those stay null, leaving 0.32% of the population without an exposure value.
  • Rural is not safe. Rural cells score lower because they have no heat island, not because heat is harmless there. Rural Poland is older and further from care; that risk runs through mechanisms this index does not measure.
Sources: GUS NSP2021 population grid and Local Data Bank; USGS Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 surface temperature; Copernicus Land Monitoring Service HRL imperviousness and tree cover density; GUGiK BDOT10k and PRG. Contains modified Copernicus Service Information.
